item.title: The Property Flipper’s Guide to Site Clearance and Quick Skip Hire
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property flipping can be an attractive way to generate returns, but the process often involves more groundwork than the glossy 'after' photos suggest. One frequently overlooked aspect is site clearance – the unglamorous but essential first step that can make or break a project's budget and timeline.

The Hidden Costs of Site Clearance

Many property investors focus on the visible transformations – new kitchens, landscaped gardens or modernised interiors. However, the initial strip-out phase often presents unexpected challenges. Older properties may contain outdated materials requiring specialist disposal, while probate homes sometimes come with decades of accumulated belongings. Underestimating clearance requirements can lead to:

  • Project delays from extended skip hire periods
  • Budget overruns due to additional waste removal
  • Hidden costs like hazardous material disposal
  • Storage fees for items awaiting clearance

Planning an Efficient Clearance Strategy

Experienced flippers typically develop systematic approaches to site clearance. Some key considerations include:

  • Waste audits: Assessing the volume and type of materials needing removal before ordering skips
  • Permit checks: Verifying local council regulations for skip placement and waste disposal
  • Recycling opportunities: Identifying salvageable materials that could be sold or donated
  • Contingency planning: Allocating extra budget and time for unexpected clearance requirements

For those new to property renovation, consulting with experienced clearance specialists might prove valuable. Many firms offer fixed-price quotes based on property size and condition, helping investors avoid unpredictable costs.

While site clearance lacks the visual appeal of later renovation stages, proper planning at this phase often determines a project's overall success. By factoring in realistic timelines and budgets for this essential first step, property investors can create more accurate project plans and protect their profit margins.

item.title: London asking rents accelerate despite falling demand
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

London’s rental market continues to defy expectations, with advertised rents rising sharply despite a noticeable drop in tenant demand. According to recent data from online agency Hello Neighbour, asking rents in the capital increased by 8.7% in July compared to the same month last year. This marks an acceleration from the 6.4% annual rise recorded in June. However, this upward trend in rental prices coincides with a decline in tenant enquiries, which fell to an average of 34 per property in July, down from 43 in June and significantly lower than the 93 enquiries recorded in July 2023.

Rising Rents Amid Falling Demand

The latest figures highlight a growing trend of rental prices climbing whilst tenant demand weakens. Hello Neighbour attributes this to a combination of reduced net migration and ongoing affordability pressures faced by renters. Despite the drop in demand, rental supply has remained stable, contributing to the upward pressure on prices. This suggests that landlords are feeling confident in their ability to secure higher rents, even as fewer tenants compete for available properties.

Another notable development is the widening gap between advertised rents and the rents landlords ultimately achieve. In July, this gap increased to 2.7 percentage points, up from 1.4 in June. This trend may be linked to recent changes introduced by the Renters’ Rights Act, which restricts landlords from accepting offers above the advertised rent and imposes tighter controls on rent increases during tenancies. As a result, landlords may be incentivised to set higher initial asking prices, knowing they cannot adjust rents as easily once a tenancy begins.

The Impact of Legislative Changes

The Renters’ Rights Act, which came into effect earlier this year, appears to be reshaping landlord behaviour in the London rental market. By limiting landlords’ ability to negotiate higher rents after a property is advertised, the legislation has encouraged a more cautious approach to pricing. Landlords may now be advertising properties at higher initial rents to safeguard against potential income restrictions during the tenancy. This could explain the growing disparity between asking rents and the rents landlords ultimately achieve.

Looking ahead, Hello Neighbour predicts that rental growth is likely to persist for the remainder of the year. The agency suggests that tenant demand may stabilise as the effects of reduced net migration begin to ease. Additionally, landlords’ responses to the Renters’ Rights Act are expected to become more established in the coming months, potentially leading to further adjustments in rental pricing strategies.

For renters navigating London’s competitive market, these trends underscore the importance of thorough research and careful budgeting. Meanwhile, landlords may wish to stay informed about legislative changes and market dynamics to make informed decisions about their rental properties.

item.title: landlord Law Newsround #448
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The start of August has brought a wave of housing-related news, with one particular issue standing out: the challenges renters face when charging electric vehicles (EVs). A recent survey highlights that tenants often encounter significant hurdles in accessing EV charging facilities, raising questions about fairness and accessibility in the rental market.

EV Charging Challenges for Renters

The survey reveals that renters are at a distinct disadvantage compared to homeowners when it comes to charging their EVs. Homeowners typically have the freedom to install charging points on their property, whilst renters must navigate complex negotiations with landlords or property management companies. This disparity could hinder the adoption of electric vehicles among tenants, especially as the UK moves towards greener transport solutions.

For landlords, this presents an opportunity to adapt to changing tenant needs. Installing EV charging points could make rental properties more appealing, particularly in urban areas where EV usage is on the rise. However, the costs and logistical challenges involved may deter some landlords from taking this step.

The Broader Implications for the Rental Market

This issue underscores a broader trend in the housing market: the growing expectation for rental properties to meet modern lifestyle demands. As EVs become more common, tenants are increasingly prioritising properties with charging facilities. Landlords who fail to address this demand risk losing out to competitors who are more forward-thinking.

Additionally, policymakers may need to consider measures to encourage landlords to invest in EV infrastructure. This could include incentives such as tax reliefs or grants, making it more financially viable for landlords to install charging points. Without such support, the gap between homeowners and renters in accessing EV facilities could widen further.

It’s worth noting that this issue also ties into the UK’s broader environmental goals. With the government aiming to phase out petrol and diesel cars by 2030, ensuring equitable access to EV charging is crucial. Renters, who make up a significant portion of the population, must not be left behind in this transition.

What This Means for Borrowers and Investors

For those considering property investment, the demand for EV-friendly rentals could influence future decisions. Properties with charging facilities may attract tenants more easily and command higher rents, potentially offering better returns for investors. Meanwhile, borrowers looking to purchase a rental property might factor in the cost of installing EV charging points when calculating their budget.

As the housing market continues to evolve, staying attuned to these trends could prove beneficial for both landlords and tenants. The growing importance of EV charging facilities is just one example of how shifting priorities are reshaping the rental landscape.

In conclusion, the challenges faced by renters in accessing EV charging facilities highlight a pressing issue in the housing market. Addressing this disparity will require collaboration between landlords, policymakers, and tenants to ensure a fair and sustainable approach to greener transport solutions.

item.title: Tenancy fraud poses £4.1bn risk to rental sector
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK’s private rental sector faces a staggering £4.1bn annual risk due to fraudulent tenancy applications, according to recent analysis by Goodlord. Examining over one million tenant references, the research revealed that 41 applications per 1,000 were flagged for suspected fraud between July 2025 and June 2026. While this marks a slight decline from the peak of 46.6 per 1,000 in late 2024, suspected fraud remains significantly higher than historical levels.

Rising Fraud Rates and Regional Variations

Goodlord’s findings highlight a sharp 40% increase in suspected fraud cases in 2025 compared to the previous year. The company estimates the average financial impact of a fraudulent tenancy at £9,601, factoring in costs such as rent arrears, legal fees, property damage, and void periods. Applying this to the UK’s 5.3 million privately rented households, assuming two tenant references per property, the potential annual exposure could reach £4.1bn.

Regional discrepancies were also evident, with London recording fraud rates nearly double the national average. The West Midlands and the North West followed closely, while overseas applications also showed higher-than-average fraud rates. Notably, properties with monthly rents exceeding £10,000 saw fraud rates nearing 18 per 1,000 applications, significantly higher than those in more affordable rental markets.

Evolving Fraud Tactics

The analysis of confirmed fraud cases in 2025 revealed a worrying trend: fake employment references surged by 226.6% year-on-year, becoming the fastest-growing category of fraud. Referee fraud and identity manipulation also saw substantial increases, rising by 146.4% and 140.4%, respectively. While these categories have slightly declined in 2026, they remain above 2024 levels.

Nishma Parekh, director of referencing at Goodlord, emphasised the growing sophistication of fraudsters. “Fraudsters are no longer relying on a single forged payslip – they’re building entire fake identities, complete with false employers and invented referees,” she explained. “The industry needs to shift from spotting individual red flags to identifying patterns throughout the referencing process.”

Parekh also stressed the importance of consistent reviews to stay ahead of evolving fraud tactics. As fraudsters continue to refine their methods, landlords and letting agents may wish to adopt more robust verification processes to mitigate risks.

Protecting the Rental Sector

With fraud posing a multi-billion-pound threat to the rental sector, stakeholders could benefit from enhanced referencing systems and greater vigilance. Implementing advanced checks, such as cross-referencing employment details and verifying referee identities, might help reduce the risk of fraudulent applications.

For landlords, staying informed about emerging fraud trends and investing in reliable referencing services could prove essential in safeguarding their properties and finances. As the rental market evolves, proactive measures may be key to maintaining trust and security for all parties involved.

item.title: Property giant combines three surveying brands into one
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Three established surveying brands have merged under a single identity as part of a strategic consolidation by property services group LRG. The newly formed MAP Chartered Surveyors combines the expertise of Stirling Ackroyd, MAP and Romans, creating a national operation with over two centuries of combined industry experience.

A unified surveying proposition

The rebrand, which took effect in early July, brings together 50 surveyors operating across regional networks throughout England. The merger pools the resources of three respected firms: 150-year-old Stirling Ackroyd, 40-year-old MAP and 35-year-old Romans. Homeowners and lenders may find the consolidated service offers greater consistency in valuation and surveying standards nationwide.

Ryan Mathews, LRG's group managing director of surveying, explained: "This unification builds on each brand's longstanding commitment to rigorous inspections and client-focused advice. While our scale increases - with over 20,000 annual inspections on £8.4bn of property - we retain the local knowledge that underpins quality surveying."

Expanding national coverage

The newly formed MAP Chartered Surveyors continues to serve over 400 business clients and 200 lenders, with LRG planning to extend its reach through its branch network. The group's recent acquisition of Northern Estate Agencies Group, adding 36 branches across northern England, is expected to generate additional surveying referrals in regions including West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester.

Neil Louth, LRG group executive director, emphasised: "Clients will benefit from the same experienced professionals delivering consistent service standards, now backed by national coverage and the resources of one of the UK's largest property services groups."

The existing management team remains unchanged following the rebrand, ensuring continuity for existing clients. For those requiring surveying services, the merger may present an opportunity to access a broader range of expertise while maintaining the personal approach associated with local providers.

item.title: Property group adds first dedicated commercial management brand
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

LRG has recently expanded its portfolio with the acquisition of CBGA Property Management, marking its first foray into dedicated commercial property management. Established in 1989, CBGA specialises in managing commercial properties across sectors such as office, industrial, retail, and leisure. The company will continue to operate under its existing name from its London and Birmingham offices, maintaining its client-focused approach.

A Strategic Addition to LRG’s Portfolio

The acquisition brings LRG an established commercial property management operation with a national client base and a UK-wide managed portfolio. CBGA’s services include property management, service charge administration, client reporting, property inspections, facilities management, health and safety compliance, and pre-purchase due diligence. This move aligns with LRG’s strategy to partner with businesses that have strong leadership teams and trusted client relationships.

Simon Worthington, Chief Strategy Officer at LRG, highlighted the value of the acquisition, stating: “CBGA Property Management is an excellent business with an experienced team, a strong national portfolio, and long-standing client relationships. Its specialist expertise in commercial property management and client accounting makes it a valuable addition to LRG.” He also confirmed that CBGA will continue to operate under its existing name, with the same management team and partner-led service.

Focus on Continuity and Growth

For CBGA’s clients and team, the acquisition ensures continuity. Richard Turner, Partner at CBGA Property Management, emphasised the importance of finding a long-term partner that recognises the strength of their existing team and client relationships. He said: “LRG shares our focus on delivering a high-quality service and brings the scale and investment to support our continued development.”

This acquisition not only strengthens LRG’s position in the commercial property market but also provides a platform for future growth. Worthington added: “As our first dedicated commercial management brand, CBGA gives us a strong foundation from which to develop our wider commercial offering.”

LRG’s strategy focuses on sustainable growth, partnering with businesses that have clear opportunities for expansion. With CBGA’s existing management team remaining in place, LRG aims to build on its newly acquired expertise to enhance its commercial property services.

This move signifies a significant step for LRG as it diversifies its portfolio and strengthens its presence in the commercial property sector.

item.title: Rightmove reveals Brit buyers’ overseas property hotspots
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For the second year running, Portugal's Algarve has emerged as the most sought-after overseas property destination for British buyers, according to Rightmove's latest analysis. The sunny coastal region maintained its top spot ahead of Paphos in Cyprus and Spain's Mallorca, rounding out a podium of perennial favourites. The ranking highlights British homeowners' enduring attraction to Mediterranean climates and relaxed lifestyles when considering properties abroad.

Mediterranean destinations dominate wish lists

Rightmove's data reveals a clear preference for sun-drenched European locations, with Spain claiming four spots in the top ten destinations. Following the Algarve, Paphos and Mallorca, France's Dordogne region took fourth place, while Spanish hotspots Alicante and Costa del Sol completed the top six. Greek islands Crete and Corfu ranked seventh and eighth respectively, with Murcia in Spain and Normandy in France rounding out the list.

At country level, Spain led the search rankings, followed by France and Italy - a trio that collectively accounts for the majority of British overseas property interest. Cyprus, Portugal and Greece filled the next three positions, with Malta, Ireland, Bulgaria and Gibraltar completing the top ten most searched nations.

Beyond holiday dreams: practical considerations

While summer browsing might begin with idyllic visions of overseas living, property professionals emphasise the importance of thorough research before committing to a purchase. NAEA Propertymark president Ian Harris notes that whilst warmer climates and lifestyle changes remain key motivators, practical considerations should form the foundation of any overseas property decision.

Prospective buyers might consider several crucial factors before taking the plunge:

  • Local property laws and ownership regulations
  • Taxation implications in both the UK and destination country
  • Residency requirements and visa restrictions
  • Ongoing maintenance and ownership costs
  • Access to healthcare and other essential services

Rightmove's overseas director Nick Robertson observes that summer holidays often serve as a research period for serious buyers: "Many use their break to explore locations properly, from assessing available property types to understanding what daily life would entail beyond the holiday atmosphere."

For those contemplating an overseas purchase, consulting regulated property professionals with local expertise could help navigate the complexities of international transactions. As the data shows, whilst the allure of Mediterranean living remains strong, informed decisions tend to yield the most successful outcomes for British buyers seeking properties abroad.

item.title: Landlords turn out in force for Renters’ Rights Act online briefing
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Over 100 landlords from Essex and Suffolk recently attended an online briefing about the Renters’ Rights Act, highlighting growing concerns about adapting to the legislation’s new requirements. The webinar, organised by estate agency Boydens, addressed key changes affecting the private rental sector, with particular focus on compliance challenges for property investors.

Key concerns for landlords under new legislation

The virtual event covered several major reforms introduced by the act, including the shift to periodic tenancies, the removal of Section 21 ‘no-fault’ evictions, and new rules governing rent increases and bidding practices. Attendees reportedly expressed significant apprehension about navigating the updated possession process when dealing with problematic tenancies.

Insurance solutions emerged as a key discussion point, with landlords exploring products that could protect against lost rental income, legal expenses and lengthy court proceedings. The high attendance figures – unusual for this period – suggest many property owners are actively seeking guidance on implementing the changes.

item.title: Property agents urged to review lone-working procedures
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Estate and letting agents across the UK are being encouraged to reassess their lone-working policies following renewed focus on workplace safety during last month’s 40th anniversary of Suzy Lamplugh’s disappearance. The tragic case of the estate agent, who vanished after attending a work appointment in 1986, continues to highlight ongoing risks for property professionals conducting viewings, valuations and inspections alone.

Updated safety guidance for property professionals

Propertymark has released updated lone-working guidance that could help agencies better protect their staff. The professional body recommends comprehensive risk assessments that consider factors such as:

  • Previous threats or disputes involving clients
  • Appointments in isolated locations with poor mobile coverage
  • Out-of-hours meetings and unexpected attendees
  • Known hazards at specific properties

The guidance stresses that employees should feel empowered to terminate or rearrange appointments if they sense potential danger. Kim Lidbury, ARLA Propertymark president, noted: "Suzy's disappearance shocked the nation and remains an event that, to this day, weighs heavily on the minds of those working within property."

Practical safety measures for agencies

Propertymark advises firms to implement several key safety protocols. Regular staff training could help workers recognise warning signs, manage conflict and exit unsafe situations appropriately. Agencies might consider establishing robust check-in systems that track:

  • Employee locations throughout the working day
  • Details of client meetings and appointments
  • Scheduled check-in times with clear escalation procedures

The guidance also recommends testing emergency equipment regularly and having backup plans for when technology fails. Structured reporting procedures for incidents ranging from threats to near misses are equally important, alongside practical support for affected staff members.

While the property sector has made safety improvements since 1986, the Suzy Lamplugh Trust - founded by Suzy's parents - continues campaigning for better personal safety awareness across all industries. Property professionals undertaking lone work may wish to familiarise themselves with the latest guidance to help minimise risks in their daily work.

item.title: Short-term home moves fall to record low
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Homeowners in England and Wales are staying put for longer than ever before, with the proportion selling within three years of purchase hitting a record low, according to new analysis. Research by Connells Group reveals just 5% of sellers in 2024 had owned their property for under three years - down from 15% in 2006 and 8% in 2016.

Changing moving patterns

The average homeowner now stays in their property for 12.3 years before selling - a significant increase from 9.2 years a decade ago. The shift is particularly noticeable in London, where only 9% of sellers had owned their home for five years or less this year, compared to 27% in 2006.

Several factors appear to be driving this trend:

  • Higher transaction costs including stamp duty
  • Increased mortgage rates making moves less affordable
  • Weaker house price growth reducing equity gains

Rising instances of negative equity

The research highlights that 20% of sellers who owned their property for five years or less made a loss in 2024, compared to just 6% in 2006. For those selling within three years, nearly a quarter (23%) sold for less than they paid - more than double the 10% figure from 2006.

The effect is particularly pronounced in the prime property market, where 32% of homes originally bought for £1m+ are now worth less than their purchase price. Across England and Wales, an estimated 7.9% of homes have fallen in value since purchase, rising to 21% in London.

Aneisha Beveridge of Connells Group commented: "Homeowners are increasingly finding that moving no longer pays. When they do move, it increasingly needs to be a bigger, longer-term decision rather than small steps on the property ladder."

The decline in property churn could have wider implications for market efficiency and labour mobility, as homeowners become more reluctant to relocate. With moving costs high and potential gains uncertain, many households appear to be opting for stability over flexibility in today's market conditions.

item.title: Property payment partnership to test synchronised completion
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

A new collaboration between PEXA and Mastercard aims to streamline the property completion process by synchronising ownership transfers and payments more effectively. The partnership will focus on utilising programmable account-to-account (A2A) payments, which could help reduce uncertainty and delays during property transactions. The proposed model would allow buyers to securely reserve funds, which are then automatically released once agreed completion conditions are met. This approach seeks to address common issues that arise when property data, legal checks, and payment flows are not aligned between the various parties involved.

How the Proposed Model Works

The initiative will be tested through Mastercard’s A2A Sandbox, a platform designed for exploring programmable payment applications. By combining PEXA’s digital property completion technology with Mastercard’s payment expertise, the partnership aims to create a more seamless and efficient process for property transactions. Vocalink, a Mastercard-owned company that operates the UK’s A2A payments infrastructure, will also support the project. This collaboration builds on PEXA’s involvement in the Bank of England Synchronisation Lab, which focuses on aligning lender fund settlements with property title transfers.

Potential Benefits for Consumers and Businesses

The partnership could bring significant improvements to the property market by making transactions more predictable and consumer-focused. Helena Forest, Executive Vice-President of Global Product and Commercial at Mastercard, highlighted the potential of A2A payment innovation to enhance efficiency and predictability in property transactions. Similarly, Krystle Kocik, UK Co-CEO at PEXA, emphasised the value of synchronised settlement and programmable payments in supporting consumers, lenders, and conveyancers. This advancement aligns with the broader goal of creating a digitally connected property market where trusted data and next-generation payment capabilities work together seamlessly.

Keith Douglas, Chief Executive of Vocalink, added that this collaboration exemplifies the UK National Payments Vision, which aims to unlock better, more coordinated payment experiences. By reducing friction and improving confidence in property transactions, this initiative could deliver tangible benefits for both individuals and businesses. As the testing phase progresses, homeowners and industry professionals may see a shift towards more efficient and secure property completions.

While the proposed model is still in its exploratory phase, it represents a promising step towards modernising the property transaction process. Borrowers and stakeholders in the property market may wish to keep an eye on developments, as this innovation could reshape how homes are bought and sold in the UK.

item.title: Ground rent cap exemption ‘could complicate leasehold sales’
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Proposed exemptions to the government's ground rent cap could introduce complications for leasehold property transactions, according to industry experts. The forthcoming Draft Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, expected in autumn 2026, aims to limit ground rents to £250 annually before reducing them to nominal "peppercorn" levels after 40 years.

What are quid pro quo leases?

The potential exemption centres on "quid pro quo" lease agreements, where homebuyers accept higher annual ground rents in exchange for a reduced upfront purchase price. Under current proposals, such leases might avoid the £250 cap if the price reduction equals or exceeds the calculated value of the higher ground rent payments.

The government is currently gathering evidence on several key aspects:

  • How prevalent these lease arrangements are in the UK property market
  • Whether they warrant special treatment under the new legislation
  • What documentation should prove a qualifying agreement exists
  • How exemptions would apply when properties change ownership

Potential impacts on property transactions

Propertymark, the professional body for estate agents, has raised concerns that the exemption could create uncertainty in the market. If introduced, freeholders would need to prove a lease qualifies, potentially requiring:

  • Original documentation showing purchase price options
  • Signed declarations from the lease's commencement or extension
  • Specialist valuation evidence for historic transactions

Such requirements might lead to disputes between freeholders and leaseholders about whether past price reductions were sufficient. The trade body warns this uncertainty could:

  • Complicate property information provided to potential buyers
  • Potentially affect mortgage lending decisions
  • Cause delays in conveyancing processes

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook has indicated exemptions would require compelling evidence, suggesting any carve-out might be narrowly defined. Propertymark has echoed this view, recommending strict criteria to prevent standard ground rents escaping the cap through loopholes.

With the legislation not expected until 2026 and the consultation ongoing, leaseholders and prospective buyers may wish to seek professional advice when considering properties with ground rent clauses. The final decision on exemptions could significantly influence both property values and transaction processes in the leasehold market.

item.title: Property team smashes charity fitness challenge
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Members of Xenia Property Group recently took part in a fitness challenge to support the Multiple Sclerosis Society, showcasing their commitment to both teamwork and charitable causes. The event, held at Manchester Central, required participants to complete ten intense workouts, ranging from a 5km run to weightlifting and rowing. The team finished the circuit in just over an hour, surpassing their target time by nearly 30 minutes.

A Test of Strength and Determination

The Deka Ignite team event proved to be a rigorous test of physical and mental endurance. Jennifer Brown, Head of Lettings at Xenia, described the experience as an opportunity to push personal limits while raising awareness for a vital cause. She highlighted the team’s determination, stating that everyone gave their all to complete the challenge in an impressive time. The event not only fostered team spirit but also helped to shine a light on the importance of supporting those affected by multiple sclerosis.

Supporting a Cause Close to Home

For Xenia Property Group, the decision to support the MS Society was deeply personal. Executive Director Farrah McWilliam shared her family’s connection to the condition, explaining how her mother’s diagnosis at a young age profoundly impacted their lives. She emphasised the importance of raising awareness and funds to support research and guidance for those living with MS. The company plans to continue its fundraising efforts throughout 2026, building on the momentum of this successful event.

Mark Haymes, Head of Community and Events Fundraising at the MS Society, expressed gratitude for Xenia’s support. With over 150,000 people in the UK living with MS, and new diagnoses occurring weekly, initiatives like this play a crucial role in advancing research and providing essential services.

Xenia Property Group’s involvement in the Deka Ignite event underscores their dedication to both charitable causes and community engagement. By combining physical challenges with fundraising, they have made a meaningful contribution to the fight against multiple sclerosis.

item.title: BTL remortgaging returns to record high
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Buy-to-let remortgaging activity has surged to record levels as landlords look to secure competitive deals amidst expiring fixed-rate products. Industry data shows a significant uptick in refinancing applications, with many property investors seeking to lock in favourable terms before potential further rate changes.

Why landlords are remortgaging now

The current spike in buy-to-let remortgage activity appears driven by several key factors:

  • A wave of fixed-rate deals taken out during the pandemic era now reaching maturity
  • Landlords aiming to mitigate higher monthly payments by securing better rates
  • Increased competition among lenders in the buy-to-let mortgage market
  • Some investors restructuring portfolios ahead of potential regulatory changes

Mortgage brokers report that landlords are being particularly proactive in reviewing their financing options, with many seeking professional advice to navigate the current market conditions. Whilst rates remain higher than the historic lows seen in recent years, there are still competitive products available for those with strong rental portfolios.

What borrowers should consider

For landlords approaching the end of their current deal, there are several aspects worth evaluating:

  • Early repayment charges on existing mortgages
  • The total cost comparison between products, not just headline rates
  • Portfolio valuation updates that might affect loan-to-value ratios
  • Stress test requirements under current affordability rules

Specialist buy-to-let mortgage advisers suggest that investors might benefit from reviewing their options several months before their current deal expires. This allows time to assess the full range of available products and potentially secure a favourable rate ahead of any market shifts.

With the buy-to-let market continuing to evolve, staying informed about financing options remains crucial for property investors. Those considering remortgaging may wish to consult an independent mortgage broker to explore the most suitable solutions for their individual circumstances.

item.title: ‘First-time buyers need more support’ – HBF
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The Home Builders Federation (HBF) has urged the government to introduce a new equity loan scheme, arguing that first-time buyers require greater support to step onto the property ladder. Their call comes after highlighting the significant economic and housing market benefits delivered by the now-closed Help to Buy scheme.

Help to Buy's lasting impact

Research from the HBF demonstrates how the Help to Buy equity loan scheme supported both homebuyers and the wider economy between 2013 and 2023. The programme enabled over 387,000 households to purchase new-build properties, with first-time buyers accounting for 84% of these transactions. Industry analysis suggests the scheme generated £23.5 billion in economic activity whilst supporting thousands of construction sector jobs.

Whilst the scheme officially closed to new applications in October 2022, its absence has left a notable gap in housing market support. The HBF argues that a replacement initiative could help address current affordability challenges, particularly for younger buyers struggling with deposit requirements in today's market.

Calls for new first-time buyer support

With average house prices remaining high relative to incomes and mortgage rates still above historic lows, many industry experts agree that first-time buyers face substantial hurdles. The HBF proposes that a fresh equity loan scheme could:

  • Reduce deposit barriers that currently prevent many from entering the market
  • Stimulate new home construction by maintaining developer confidence
  • Support regional economic growth through housing-led regeneration
  • Provide a responsible alternative to high loan-to-value mortgage products

Homebuilders stress that any new scheme should focus particularly on first-time buyers, potentially with regional price caps to ensure help reaches those who need it most. Some industry commentators suggest learning from Help to Buy's limitations, such as revising eligibility criteria to prevent price inflation in certain markets.

Mortgage brokers note that whilst various 95% LTV products exist, government-backed equity loans typically offer more favourable repayment terms than traditional high-LTV mortgages. This makes them particularly valuable during periods of economic uncertainty when buyers may be wary of stretching their budgets.

The road ahead

As the housing market continues to adjust to higher interest rates, the debate around first-time buyer support remains prominent. Industry leaders argue that well-designed housing schemes can serve as economic stabilisers whilst helping younger generations achieve homeownership.

Prospective buyers may wish to consult independent mortgage advisers to explore all available options, from shared ownership schemes to family-assisted mortgages. With housing policy likely to feature prominently in the run-up to the next general election, further developments in this area could emerge in coming months.

item.title: BTR starts on site down 79%
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK's build-to-rent (BTR) sector has seen a dramatic 79% year-on-year decline in new construction starts, according to recent industry analysis. This sharp contraction reflects growing challenges around development viability and policy uncertainty in the private rental sector.

What's Behind the Construction Slowdown?

Several factors appear to be contributing to the significant drop in new BTR projects breaking ground. Construction costs remain elevated whilst financing expenses have risen substantially with higher interest rates. Planning delays and the potential for changing rental sector regulations may also be causing developers to pause new schemes.

The slowdown follows several years of strong growth in the BTR sector, which had become an increasingly important part of the UK's housing mix. Professional landlords and institutional investors had been expanding their portfolios to meet rising tenant demand for high-quality rental accommodation.

Potential Implications for Renters

With fewer new rental homes entering the pipeline, existing tenants might face:

  • Reduced choice in the rental market
  • Potential upward pressure on rents as supply growth slows
  • Fewer opportunities to access newer, purpose-built rental properties

Industry experts suggest this development slowdown could exacerbate existing supply challenges in the private rental sector. The BTR sector had been expected to play a key role in addressing the UK's rental housing shortage, particularly in major urban areas.

The current situation highlights the sensitivity of housing development to economic conditions and policy environments. As stakeholders monitor these trends, the coming months may prove crucial for understanding whether this represents a temporary pause or a more fundamental shift in the BTR sector's growth trajectory.

item.title: Partnership completes 6-day property transaction
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A recent property purchase in Swansea has made headlines after being completed in just six days, thanks to a streamlined conveyancing process. This speedy transaction highlights how efficient collaboration between solicitors, lenders, and estate agents can significantly reduce the time it takes to buy a home.

The Fast-Track Process

Traditionally, property transactions in the UK can take several weeks or even months to complete, often due to delays in paperwork, legal checks, and communication between parties. However, this particular purchase was facilitated by a partnership that prioritised efficiency and clear communication. By leveraging digital tools and a coordinated approach, the conveyancing process was accelerated without compromising on thoroughness or compliance.

The use of technology played a key role in this record-breaking transaction. Online platforms allowed for instant sharing of documents and real-time updates, minimising the need for physical paperwork and postal delays. Additionally, all parties involved worked closely to ensure that queries were resolved promptly, further speeding up the process.

What This Means for Homebuyers

Whilst a six-day completion is exceptional, this case demonstrates that faster property transactions are achievable with the right approach. Homebuyers may wish to explore conveyancing services that prioritise efficiency, particularly if they are working to tight deadlines or aiming to move quickly.

It could also be worth considering lenders and estate agents who embrace digital solutions, as these can help streamline the process. Borrowers might find that opting for a mortgage provider with a reputation for quick turnaround times can further reduce delays.

Potential Challenges

Despite the success of this transaction, it’s important to note that not all property purchases can be completed so swiftly. Factors such as chain-free sales, straightforward mortgage approvals, and cooperative parties played a significant role in this case. For buyers in complex chains or those relying on government schemes like Help to Buy, the process may still take longer.

Additionally, whilst speed is desirable, it’s crucial to ensure that all legal checks and documentation are thoroughly completed. Cutting corners can lead to complications down the line, so homeowners may wish to balance efficiency with diligence.

This record-breaking transaction in Swansea serves as a reminder of how technology and collaboration can transform the property-buying process. Whilst not every purchase will be completed in six days, it highlights the potential for smoother and faster transactions in the future.

item.title: Buying Overseas Through a UK Company? The Paper Trail Starts Before the Offer
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Purchasing overseas property through a UK company has become an increasingly popular option for British investors. This approach can offer several advantages, particularly in light of recent changes to UK property laws, such as the stamp duty surcharge on second homes and the complexities introduced by the Renters’ Rights Act. However, navigating this process requires careful planning and a thorough understanding of the legal and financial implications.

Why Consider Buying Overseas Property Through a UK Company?

One of the primary reasons investors may opt to purchase overseas property through a UK company is the potential tax efficiency. By holding the property within a corporate structure, investors might be able to mitigate certain tax liabilities, such as inheritance tax and capital gains tax. Additionally, this approach can provide greater flexibility in managing the property, especially if it is intended for rental income or resale.

Countries like Dubai have emerged as attractive destinations for UK investors due to their favourable property market conditions and relatively straightforward buying processes. However, it is crucial to seek professional advice to ensure compliance with both UK and local regulations.

The Importance of Early Planning

For those considering this route, the paper trail begins well before making an offer. Setting up a UK company specifically for the purpose of purchasing overseas property involves several steps, including registering the company, opening a business bank account, and securing the necessary financing. Investors must also ensure that the company structure aligns with their long-term goals and complies with relevant tax laws.

Documentation is another critical aspect of the process. Investors will need to prepare a range of legal and financial documents, such as company incorporation certificates, proof of funds, and property purchase agreements. Engaging solicitors and tax advisors with expertise in international property transactions can help streamline this process and avoid costly mistakes.

Key Considerations Before Proceeding

Before embarking on the journey of purchasing overseas property through a UK company, borrowers might wish to consider the following:

  • The cost of setting up and maintaining a UK company, including annual filing fees and accounting expenses.
  • The tax implications in both the UK and the country where the property is located.
  • The potential impact of currency fluctuations on mortgage repayments and rental income.
  • The legal requirements for owning property in the chosen overseas market.

Taking the time to research and plan thoroughly can help investors make informed decisions and maximise the benefits of their overseas property investment.

Ultimately, buying overseas property through a UK company can be a viable strategy for investors seeking to diversify their portfolios and potentially reduce their tax burden. However, this approach requires careful consideration and professional guidance to ensure a smooth and successful transaction.

item.title: Unexpected costs hit 95% of homebuyers, research reveals
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent research highlights that a staggering 95% of UK homebuyers have faced unexpected costs during their property transactions, a sharp increase from 62% just a year ago. While professional fees such as those charged by conveyancers and estate agents were found to be transparent in most cases, the study suggests that uncertainty surrounding the transaction process itself is the primary culprit behind these unforeseen expenses. This revelation comes amidst growing concerns about the complexity and stress of moving home.

The Rise of Unexpected Costs

The research, conducted by PEXA and based on a survey of over 1,000 UK homebuyers, found that 64% of respondents described these unexpected costs as significant. Nearly half (47%) believed these expenses could have been avoided entirely. Interestingly, the issue does not appear to stem from professional fees, with 85% of participants stating that conveyancer fees were clear and 79% expressing the same view about estate agent fees. Instead, the problem lies in the incremental nature of additional costs, which often arise as the transaction progresses.

Stress and Delays in the Home-Moving Process

The study also sheds light on the stress and delays associated with moving home. A significant 83% of respondents described the process as stressful, citing fragmented procedures, repeated checks, and disconnected organisations as key contributors. There was also a notable gap between expectations and reality when it came to transaction times. While homebuyers anticipated the process would take around four months from offer acceptance to moving in, wider market data reveals that it often extends to seven or eight months.

Calls for Greater Transparency and Efficiency

The findings align with the government’s recent publication of the Home Buying and Selling Reform Roadmap, which aims to improve transparency and connectivity across property transactions. Industry experts have emphasised the importance of addressing uncertainty rather than focusing solely on speeding up the process. Krystle Kocik, UK co-CEO of PEXA, stated that achieving certainty depends on better information, verified identities, secure fund movements, and connected legal ownership transfers throughout the transaction.

Alison Verlander, director of mortgages at UK Finance, echoed this sentiment, highlighting the need for better upfront information, reusable verified data, and clearer visibility across the transaction. Stephen Ward, director of strategy and external relations at the Council for Licensed Conveyancers, added that consumers value professional expertise but also expect clearer communication, greater transparency, and a more predictable experience.

As the property industry continues to evolve, it is clear that a combination of legal expertise and efficient digital processes will be key to creating a smoother, more transparent home-moving experience for buyers and sellers alike.
